:::

::: {.puzzle}
Thread beads on a tight string and join its two ends into a ring, so that every bead has a neighbor on each side and none is special. Pluck one bead. The motion looks like a tangle. Yet it is made of a handful of perfectly regular motions, all happening at once. What are they, and how do you find them?
:::

Watch the tangle after one bead is plucked. Then press the mode buttons one at a time.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <canvas id="rCanvas" style="height:300px" aria-label="Beads on a ring, displacements drawn in and out of the circle"></canvas>
  <div class="slider"><label for="rN">Beads N</label><input type="range" id="rN" min="3" max="24" step="1" value="8"><output id="rNo"></output></div>
  <div class="controls" id="rModes" role="group" aria-label="Play one mode"></div>
  <div class="controls"><button id="rPluck">Pluck one bead</button><button id="rPlay" class="primary">Hear this motion</button></div>
  <svg class="spec" id="rSpec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" style="max-width:520px" aria-label="Frequencies of the modes relative to the lowest"></svg>
  <div class="readout" id="rRead"></div>
  <p class="cap">Displacements are drawn in and out of the circle so you can see them; on a real ring the beads move up and down, out of the page. Mode k is a wave that fits k times around the ring. Stems (the vertical lines): frequencies of the modes as multiples of mode 1's frequency, with height showing how much of each mode the current motion contains.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

::: {.gist}
**The gist.** Each regular motion is a wave that fits a whole number of times around the ring. In it, every bead swings at the same frequency and the shape never changes, as if the whole ring were one mass on a spring. Such a motion is called a [mode](glossary.qmd#mode). The tangle is all the modes at once, each at its own frequency: a chord. Press "Hear this motion" on the tangle, then on a single mode.
:::

## On the pitch ruler

The stems are the modes' frequencies, as multiples of mode 1's, the slowest wave that swings back and forth (mode 0 just drifts: the whole ring moves together). Each stem's height is how much of that mode the current motion contains. Apart from mode 1 itself, they are not on the lines. With 8 beads, as the demo starts, the modes sit at 1×, 1.85×, 2.41× and 2.61×. Raise the number of beads and the low stems close in on the lines: with 24 beads, modes 2 and 3 are within 2.5% of 2× and 3×. The high modes stay far off.

## How it works

**Each bead is pulled toward its neighbors.** The string on each side of a bead pulls along itself. When the bead sits above both neighbors, the two pulls together point down, and the further it sits above their average, the harder it is pulled back. So each bead is a mass on a spring, except that where its spring pulls it depends on where its neighbors are.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Step-by-step derivation</span>The force on one bead <span class="needs">uses derivatives and a small-angle approximation</span></summary>

Let $u_j$ be the height of bead $j$, with beads spaced $h$ apart along a string of tension $T$, each of mass $m$. Because the loop closes, bead $N$ is next to bead 1, so indices are counted around the ring. (This is an idealization: a real loop of string would need something to hold it out against its own tension. The model keeps only the sideways pulls between neighbors, exactly as for a straight string whose two ends are joined.) For small displacements, Newton's law for bead $j$ is
$$
m\,\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}\left(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}\right).
$$

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 420 160" role="img" aria-label="A bead pulled by the string toward its two neighbors">
  <path class="dash" d="M 20 120 L 400 120"/>
  <path class="ink" d="M 60 110 L 210 60 L 360 100"/>
  <circle cx="60" cy="110" r="6" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="210" cy="60" r="7" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="360" cy="100" r="6" class="fillacc"/>
  <path class="pos" d="M 210 60 L 150 80"/><path class="pos" d="M 210 60 L 270 76"/>
  <path class="neg" d="M 210 60 L 210 110"/>
  <text x="40" y="140">bead j−1</text><text x="190" y="40">bead j</text><text x="340" y="140">bead j+1</text>
  <text x="120" y="76">T</text><text x="280" y="70">T</text><text x="218" y="100">net pull</text>
</svg>
```

1. The string between beads $j$ and $j+1$ pulls bead $j$ along itself with force $T$.
2. Its slope is $(u_{j+1} - u_j)/h$. Let $\theta$ be the angle that piece of string makes with the horizontal. For small slopes the vertical part of the pull is $T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta = T(u_{j+1} - u_j)/h$.
3. The string on the other side contributes $T(u_{j-1} - u_j)/h$.
4. Adding the two and applying Newton's law gives the equation above. The bracket $u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}$ is twice the gap between the average of the neighbors and bead $j$ itself: a bead sitting above its neighbors is pulled down, one sitting below is pulled up.

The assumptions are small slopes and a tension that does not change as the string flexes.

</details>
:::

**All the beads at once: a matrix.** Write all the heights as one list. Then the forces on all the beads at once come from one table of numbers, a matrix, applied to that list; this matrix is the ring's operator. A shape that the matrix only rescales, without changing it, is called an [eigenvector](glossary.qmd#eigenvector), and the rescaling factor is its [eigenvalue](glossary.qmd#eigenvalue). Each eigenvector is a mode: the beads swing in that shape like a single mass on a spring, and the eigenvalue, times a fixed constant, plays the part of the spring's stiffness divided by its mass, so the mode's frequency comes from its square root. The list of all the eigenvalues is the matrix's [spectrum](glossary.qmd#spectrum).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Step-by-step derivation</span>The matrix, its eigenvectors, and why each one is a mode <span class="needs">uses matrices</span></summary>

**The matrix.** Collect the heights into a column $u = (u_1, \dots, u_N)$. The equations for all beads at once read $\ddot u = -\frac{T}{mh}\,K u$, where $K$ is the $N\times N$ matrix with 2 on the diagonal, $-1$ just above and below it, and $-1$ in the two corners, because bead 1 and bead $N$ are neighbors. For $N = 5$,
$$
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Here $Ku$ is the column whose $j$-th entry is row $j$ of $K$ times $u$: multiply each entry of row $j$ by the matching entry of $u$, and add. Row $j$ has 2 in place $j$ and $-1$ in places $j - 1$ and $j + 1$, so $(Ku)_j = 2u_j - u_{j-1} - u_{j+1}$, and the matrix equation is the bead equation for every bead at once. Each row of $K$ is the row above shifted one place to the right, wrapping around; a matrix with this property is called [circulant](glossary.qmd#circulant).

**Eigenvectors and eigenvalues.** A nonzero column $v$ is an eigenvector of $K$, with eigenvalue $\lambda$, if $Kv = \lambda v$: the matrix only rescales it, possibly by zero. The set of all eigenvalues is the spectrum of $K$.

**Modes.** If $Kv = \lambda v$, then $u(t) = v\cos(\omega t)$ is a motion of the beads, provided $\omega^2 = \frac{T}{mh}\lambda$. To check, differentiate twice: $\ddot u = -\omega^2 v\cos\omega t$, while $-\frac{T}{mh}Ku = -\frac{T}{mh}\lambda v\cos\omega t$. Every bead swings at the same [angular frequency](glossary.qmd#angular-frequency) $\omega$ (radians per second; page 1), in the fixed shape $v$. This is the mass on a spring again, once for each eigenvector.

**A small example, three beads.** For $N = 3$,
$$
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Row $j$ of this $K$ gives $(Kv)_j = 3v_j - (v_1 + v_2 + v_3)$. The column $(1, 1, 1)$ gives $K(1,1,1) = (0,0,0)$, so it is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0: every bead moves up together, nothing stretches, nothing pulls back, and the frequency is 0, so the ring just drifts. Any column whose entries add up to zero gives $(Kv)_j = 3v_j$, so $Kv = 3v$. Every such column is a combination $a(1, -1, 0) + b(0, 1, -1)$, so these eigenvectors fill a whole plane: every one is built from those two shapes, and neither of the two is a multiple of the other. The eigenvalues are $0, 3, 3$, with 3 counted twice: it has [multiplicity](glossary.qmd#multiplicity) 2.

</details>
:::

**The modes are waves around the ring.** On a ring no bead is special, so the eigenvectors are waves that fit a whole number of times around: a wave with one crest, two crests, three, and so on. A wave with more crests bends more sharply from bead to bead, so each bead is pulled back harder and the wave swings faster. Splitting a motion into these waves is the [discrete Fourier transform](glossary.qmd#dft). In the 1730s Daniel Bernoulli studied systems like this, weights strung along a flexible thread and a hanging chain, and came to believe that every vibration is built from such simple motions; in 1753 he put this forward as a general principle.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Step-by-step derivation</span>The waves and their eigenvalues, for any number of beads <span class="needs">uses trigonometric identities</span></summary>

Try the column $v_j = \cos(2\pi jk/N)$, a wave with $k$ crests around the ring. The identity $\cos(a + b) + \cos(a - b) = 2\cos a\cos b$, with $a = 2\pi jk/N$ and $b = 2\pi k/N$, gives $v_{j+1} + v_{j-1} = 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\,v_j$, so
$$
(Kv)_j = 2v_j - v_{j+1} - v_{j-1} = \big(2 - 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\big)\,v_j = 4\sin^2\!\Big(\frac{\pi k}{N}\Big)\,v_j ,
$$
using $1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^2 x$. The same holds for $v_j = \sin(2\pi jk/N)$. These are the shapes the mode buttons play, and the eigenvalues are $4\sin^2(\pi k/N)$. At the beads, a wave with $N - k$ crests looks exactly like one with $k$ crests (the cosine is the same and the sine changes sign), so the different eigenvalues come from $k = 0, 1, \dots$ up to $N/2$, rounded down, and each one from $k = 1$ up to just below $N/2$ has two eigenvectors, a cosine and a sine. (At $k = 0$, and at $k = N/2$ when $N$ is even, the sine is zero at every bead, so only the cosine is left.) Writing any motion as a sum of these waves splits it into separate masses on springs, one per wave; that splitting is the discrete Fourier transform.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Complex form</span>The same waves as $e^{2\pi i jk/N}$ <span class="needs">uses complex numbers</span></summary>

With [Euler's formula](glossary.qmd#euler-formula) $e^{ix} = \cos x + i\sin x$, the cosine and sine waves combine into $v_j = e^{2\pi i jk/N}$ for $k = 0, 1, \dots, N - 1$ (here $i$ is the imaginary unit and $j$ the bead number). Then $(Kv)_j = \big(2 - e^{2\pi ik/N} - e^{-2\pi ik/N}\big)v_j = 4\sin^2(\pi k/N)\,v_j$ in one line. These $N$ waves are the basis vectors of the discrete Fourier transform, and they are eigenvectors of every circulant matrix, not only this one. Combined with the time factor $e^{\mp i\omega t}$, the waves with $k$ and $N - k$ crests travel around the ring in opposite directions.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Proof</span>Every motion is a sum of modes <span class="needs">uses linear algebra</span></summary>

The matrix $K$ is symmetric: the entry in row $i$, column $j$ equals the entry in row $j$, column $i$. By the [spectral theorem for symmetric matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem), $K$ has a basis of $N$ mutually [orthogonal](glossary.qmd#orthogonal) (perpendicular) eigenvectors $v^{(1)}, \dots, v^{(N)}$ with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N$. Write the motion as $u(t) = \sum_k a_k(t)\,v^{(k)}$. Substituting into $\ddot u = -\frac{T}{mh}Ku$ and taking the dot product with $v^{(k)}$, which removes every other term because they are perpendicular, gives $\ddot a_k = -\omega_k^2 a_k$ with $\omega_k^2 = \frac{T}{mh}\lambda_k$: each coefficient obeys its own mass-on-a-spring equation. With starting shape $u(0) = \sum_k c_k v^{(k)}$ and starting velocity $\dot u(0) = \sum_k d_k v^{(k)}$, and by the uniqueness of solutions from page 1, every motion is $u(t) = \sum_k \big(c_k\cos\omega_k t + \frac{d_k}{\omega_k}\sin\omega_k t\big)v^{(k)}$, read as $c_k + d_k t$ when $\omega_k = 0$. The eigenvalues are nonnegative because $u \cdot Ku = \sum_j u_j(2u_j - u_{j+1} - u_{j-1}) = \sum_j (u_{j+1} - u_j)^2 \ge 0$, by regrouping the terms around the ring; for an eigenvector this equals $\lambda\,(u\cdot u)$.

</details>
:::

**Almost whole numbers.** A long wave, with few crests, spreads over many beads, and to it the beads look like a smooth string; its frequency grows in step with its number of crests, almost exactly as whole numbers do. A short wave, with crests only a bead or two apart, feels the gaps between the beads, and its frequency falls behind. That is why the low stems sit near the lines and close in as you add beads, while the high ones stay off.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>How near to whole numbers <span class="needs">uses the sine function</span></summary>

By the eigenvalues above, mode $k$ has angular frequency $\omega_k = 2\sqrt{T/(mh)}\,\sin(\pi k/N)$, so its frequency is proportional to $\sin(\pi k/N)$, which is not proportional to $k$: the beads are not exactly harmonic. For small $k$, $\sin(\pi k/N) \approx \pi k/N$, so the low modes are nearly harmonic, and the ratio $\sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N)$ tends to $k$ as $N$ grows. The modes near $k = N/2$ stay far from the whole-number grid: the largest ratio is $1/\sin(\pi/N)$, about $N/\pi$, not $N/2$.

</details>
:::

## What we found

Many coupled masses move in a few special shapes, modes, each swinging at its own frequency like a single mass on a spring. Finding them means finding the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of a matrix, the ring's operator, whose list of eigenvalues, its spectrum, gives the frequencies. On a ring the modes are waves, and their frequencies sit near the lines of the pitch ruler, but not on them.

## The next puzzle

The low frequencies of the beads are almost whole-number multiples of the lowest, and they get closer as you add beads. What happens with infinitely many beads, a continuous loop of string? Do the frequencies land exactly on the lines? And can every shape of the loop be built from these waves?

Wikipedia, [Circulant matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circulant_matrix), [Discrete Fourier transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_Fourier_transform), [Normal mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_mode) and [Spectral theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem).

```{=html}
<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core, N = 8, a = [], b = [], u0 = null, t0 = performance.now(), mode = 1;
  var cv = document.getElementById("rCanvas"), ctx = cv.getContext("2d");
  function lam(k) { return 4 * Math.pow(Math.sin(Math.PI * k / N), 2); }
  function ratio(k) { return Math.sin(Math.PI * k / N) / Math.sin(Math.PI / N); }
  function setMode(k) {
    mode = k; a = []; b = []; for (var q = 0; q < N; q++) { a.push(0); b.push(0); }
    a[k] = 1; t0 = performance.now(); buttons(); spec();
  }
  function pluck() {
    // bead 0 pushed out by 1, the others at rest: u_j = (1/N) sum_k e^{2 pi i jk/N}, folded into cosines
    mode = -1; a = []; b = [];
    for (var k = 0; k < N; k++) { a.push(k === 0 ? 1 / N : (2 * k < N ? 2 / N : 0)); b.push(0); }
    if (N % 2 === 0) a[N / 2] = 1 / N;
    t0 = performance.now(); buttons(); spec();
  }
  function shape(t) {
    var u = [];
    for (var j = 0; j < N; j++) {
      var s = 0;
      for (var k = 0; k <= Math.floor(N / 2); k++) {
        var w = 2 * Math.PI * 0.35 * ratio(k), c = Math.cos(w * t);
        s += (a[k] * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * j * k / N) + b[k] * Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * j * k / N)) * (k === 0 ? 1 : c);
      }
      u.push(s);
    }
    return u;
  }
  function buttons() {
    var box = document.getElementById("rModes"); box.innerHTML = "";
    for (var k = 0; k <= Math.floor(N / 2); k++) (function (k) {
      var bt = document.createElement("button"); bt.type = "button"; bt.textContent = "mode " + k; bt.setAttribute("aria-pressed", k === mode);
      bt.addEventListener("click", function () { setMode(k); }); box.appendChild(bt);
    })(k);
  }
  function spec() {
    var parts = [];
    for (var k = 1; k <= Math.floor(N / 2); k++) parts.push({ ratio: ratio(k), amp: Math.max(Math.abs(a[k]), Math.abs(b[k]), 0.0001) });
    C.stems(document.getElementById("rSpec"), parts, { W: 320, H: 100, rmax: Math.max(4, Math.ceil(ratio(Math.floor(N / 2)))), fs: 8, sw: 3 });
    var r = []; for (var k = 1; k <= Math.min(5, Math.floor(N / 2)); k++) r.push(ratio(k).toFixed(3));
    document.getElementById("rRead").innerHTML = "N = <b>" + N + "</b> · eigenvalues 4 sin&sup2;(&pi;k/N) · frequency ratios <b>" + r.join(", ") + "</b>" + (mode === 0 ? " · mode 0 has eigenvalue 0: the ring shifts as a whole and nothing pulls it back" : "");
  }
  function draw(now) {
    var d = C.fit(cv), W = cv.width, H = cv.height, cx = W / 2, cy = H / 2, R = Math.min(W, H) * 0.32, t = (now - t0) / 1000, u = shape(t), mx = 1;
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--grid"); ctx.lineWidth = d; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(cx, cy, R, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); ctx.lineWidth = 1.5 * d; ctx.beginPath();
    for (var j = 0; j <= N; j++) { var jj = j % N, th = 2 * Math.PI * jj / N - Math.PI / 2, r = R + u[jj] / mx * R * 0.28, x = cx + r * Math.cos(th), y = cy + r * Math.sin(th); if (j) ctx.lineTo(x, y); else ctx.moveTo(x, y); }
    ctx.stroke();
    for (var j = 0; j < N; j++) { var th = 2 * Math.PI * j / N - Math.PI / 2, r = R + u[j] / mx * R * 0.28; ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(cx + r * Math.cos(th), cy + r * Math.sin(th), 6 * d, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.fill(); }
    requestAnimationFrame(draw);
  }
  document.getElementById("rPlay").addEventListener("click", function () {
    // the model has no friction; the sound is faded out only so that it stops
    var parts = []; for (var k = 1; k <= Math.floor(N / 2); k++) parts.push({ f: 196 * ratio(k), amp: Math.max(Math.abs(a[k]), Math.abs(b[k])), tau: 0.8 });
    if (!parts.some(function (p) { return p.amp > 1e-6; })) parts = [{ f: 1, amp: 0, tau: 1 }];
    C.play(C.render(parts, 2.2), 0.7);
  });
  document.getElementById("rPluck").addEventListener("click", pluck);
  var ns = document.getElementById("rN");
  ns.addEventListener("input", function () { N = parseInt(ns.value, 10); document.getElementById("rNo").textContent = N; if (mode < 0) pluck(); else setMode(Math.min(mode, Math.floor(N / 2))); });
  document.getElementById("rNo").textContent = N;
  C.onTheme(spec);
  pluck(); requestAnimationFrame(draw);
})();
</script>
```
